rv.q: Linton’s richly textured production reclaims him as a major voice.

Watching this revival of Alterations by Michael Abbensetts, rediscovered as part of the Black Plays Archive at the National Theatre, you do wonder how many other great pieces of writing are gathering dust somewhere.

Though lacking the depth and intricacy to make it a truly great play, given a few tucks itself by playwright Trish Cooke, it’s a lively comedy about Black British life that springs into life in Lynette Linton’s warm, exuberant production.
Genial, larky, with small touches of melancholy, Alterations is more atmospheric than incisive.
It ultimately feels like a nicely observed but relatively slight slice of life drama.
Uneven revival of pioneering Black playwright Michael Abbensetts’ rarely produced 1978 comedy, directed by Lynette Linton and starring Arinzé Kene and Cherrelle Skeete
Sadly, however, the script tries to squeeze too many themes into a rambunctious sitcom-style format.
This is a glorious revival that proves Abbensetts’s work deserves and needs to continue to be seen.
The play has a subtle sadness to it, a sense of hopes betrayed but also achieved.
Fortunately, everyone’s acting, especially that of Kene, fills the space with laughs, hopes and disappointments that aren’t too distant from our own age.
When combined with a stage that rotates between the front and back of Walker’s shop so many times that I couldn’t help but think of the New Scotland Yard sign, it was frankly rather dizzying.
Despite its shortcomings, its lightweight quality, and its uneasy fit in this theatre space, Alterations offers an enjoyable evening that reiterates the experiences of migration in 1970s London.
This programming of work from the National Theatre Archive is vital in providing a platform for all the voices and experiences that should be reflected in contemporary British society.

cn.t: A worthy revival of Abbensetts' 1978 play sheds light on the Windrush experience, with Kene's blazing performance anchoring this engaging period piece, though the script sometimes struggles to balance its multiple themes within a sitcom structure.
